speechtext: On the orders of -the day:

subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT IN TORONTO AND HAMILTON
speechtext:
May
I direct a question to the Minister of Labour, of which I sent him notice earlier in the day? Has Toronto's serious unemployment problem received consideration by the government, and if so what relief does the government propose?

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: UNEMPLOYMENT IN TORONTO AND HAMILTON
speechtext:
I thank the hon. member for sending me notice of the question. I should add that other members in the Toronto and greater Toronto area have brought this matter to my attention, both since the house opened and before it opened.
The situation in Toronto, as reported to me this morning, is showing definite evidence of improvement, which is indicated by a fall of 700 in the total number of applicants for jobs between February 21 and 28 last. The less buoyant situation in regard to the employment in Toronto and, indeed, in Ontario, has been receiving constant attention during the winter. While the seasonal dip has been much greater in this area during the past winter than in the immediately preceding winter, all the reports I have received indicate that the unemployment is to a very large
(Mr. Chevrier.]

degree seasonal, and I am confident that by early summer the demand will be for more workers.
Unemployment insurance regular benefits, plus supplementary allowances provided for two years ago by parliamentary action in amending the Unemployment Insurance Act, are alleviating the situation very greatly. During December, 1951, and January, 1952, the total insurance payments in the city of Toronto were $1,671,631.20. It is true that unemployment insurance benefits leave a problem for the city in caring for those who could not accept work if work were available, and a comparatively small number who are not entitled to unemployment insurance benefits for several reasons, including (1) having been paid all benefits to which they are entitled; (2) benefits not yet being due; (3) cases where the amount paid under the Unemployment Insurance Act is insufficient to meet the needs of the family.
I am happy to say that in Toronto the number in this fringe class has shown a considerable reduction in February as compared with January, the figures given me this morning by representatives of the city of Toronto being 295 families in February as compared with 517 families in January.
This morning my colleague the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (Mr. Harris) and I had a very helpful discussion with representatives from Toronto and Hamilton on this problem. Those attending on behalf of Toronto were Controller David Balfour, Controller Ford Brand; from Hamilton, Mayor Lloyd Jackson, Controller Samuel Lawrence and Controller H. Arnott Hicks.
Throughout the discussion both delegations expressed the belief that the unemployment insurance commission could, under its existing powers, do more to cope with the present situation than it is now doing. I therefore asked that a member of the commission go to these two cities to hold such hearings or investigations as are necessary to ensure that maximum benefits are being derived under the Unemployment Insurance Act and regulations, and to report thereon. This the commission has agreed to do at a very early date.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

speechtext:
The house resumed, from Monday, March 3, consideration in committee of the following resolution:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure for the control and extirpation of foot-and-mouth disease and to provide in connection therewith for the payment of compensation, out of moneys appropriated by parliament, to the owners of animals slaughtered, and also in respect of any buildings, fodder, grain or other things ordered to be destroyed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should first like to ask the leader of the opposition whether he wishes to proceed further with the remarks he was making last evening, or

whether, before he proceeds, he wishes me to answer some of the questions that were asked last evening.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: In view of the fact that there were a number of questions and that the Minister of Agriculture has had the opportunity to check some of the details with his department, I think it may be best if he deals with those questions; then any remarks I might have to make could follow. It may well be that some of the answers he now has will deal with the very point that 1 proposed to raise.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
First, in order to give the house the complete record, as nearly as it is possible to do so, of what has happened up to date in connection with either foot-and-mouth disease or any other disease which may have been checked in the area, I should like to read this into the record.
Mr. Waas, of McLean, on or about November 26, called Dr. Richards of Indian Head, who prescribed for vesicular stomatitis. Dr. Hunter of Regina was called by Mr. Waas and agreed that it was vesicular stomatitis and continued the treatment. Then Mr. Waas reported to provincial veterinarian Dr. Johnson a day or so later, who agreed it was stomatitis.
Information was given by Dr. Johnson to Dr. Christie, who is in charge of our branch at Regina, on December 1. On December 2, Dr. James went out, on instructions from Dr. Christie, to investigate, and he carried on part of the check which was indicated to the house yesterday as the proper procedure in such cases. In other words, he injected some of the material into the tongue of a horse, and vesicular stomatitis developed as a result of that injection. I understand that this is taken by veterinarians to indicate that it was vesicular stomatitis and not foot-and-mouth disease. Then he examined the animals and pronounced it stomatitis. He reported his findings to Dr. Christie, and was sent cut the next day to quarantine the place; that is, he was there and made the examinations on December 2 and quarantined the place on December 3.
Dr. James then examined herds in the surrounding area and did not find any traces of the disease at that time. Dr. James reported the same disease in Smith's herd on December 7. Smith was a neighbour of Mr. Waas who assisted Mr. Waas in treating his stock. The disease appeared in the herd of Mr. Wood on December 12. Mr. Wood was another neighbour who assisted Mr. Waas in treating his stock.
Dr. James again covered the surrounding herds and found nothing further. Later in
Foot-and-mouth disease December a herd was found north and west toward Lumsden and in the vicinity of Was-cana creek-

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: What was the date?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I have not the exact date, but it was within, a few days of that time. As to the farms at McLean-that is the farms of Mr. Wood, Mr. Smith and Mr. Waas-the farm of Mr. Waas was cleared on December 8. It was found there was no further indication of the disease on December 8 and his farm was cleared. The farm of Mr. Wood was cleared on December 27, and that of Mr. Smith on December 27-[DOT]both the same day. This same disease appeared in the Bums feed lot in the latter part of December, and the feed lot was quarantined on December 28 for stomatitis. Nothing was allowed to go out of the yard until the quarantine was lifted on January 17. Any animals which did go out of the Burns yards within a reasonable time were traced and evidence secured that none of them turned out to be carriers.
Dr. Childs was out in Regina speaking to the livestock association on January 17. He discussed with our officials the matter of the disease which had been prevalent. He was at the livestock association annual meeting for the purpose of discussing certain diseases in horses, and Newcastle disease. He was not approached at the meeting by anyone who represented that foot-and-mouth disease existed in that area. He did, however, discuss the question of the investigations that had been made into stomatitis, and satisfied himself that it was not other than as it had been diagnosed.
On February 13 our branch at Regina reported through Dr. Hall-who, I may say, is assistant to Dr. Childs, and1 was in charge while Dr. Childs was away, first in order to attend this meeting at Regina, and later to take his usual statutory vacation-that the disease was taking on a more serious appearance. Samples of material were collected and sent to Hull, to Dr. Mitchell, on February 14, arriving here on the 16th. On the 16th Dr. Childs returned. On or about the 16th the samples were used on horses, cattle and swine, as suggested.
By February 18, indications were that the disease might be foot-and-mouth disease. I would say that on the 18th checks were made on cattle, swine and horses in Regina under the direction of Dr. Childs, and the report later was that there was no reaction to those injections.
I should have said that Dr. Childs left here on the 16th and flew to Regina, and was in Regina on the 17th. That is the occasion on which he went to Regina officially to deal

Foot-and-mouth disease with this matter. He put in that day and until Wednesday night in the area. He spent Sunday in consultation with Drs. Christie and Carlson. This convinced him there was a serious condition. He quarantined six municipalities on Monday, February 18. This was increased to ten by Wednesday, when the quarantine was confirmed by order in council at Ottawa. The quarantine was actually in effect on Monday. The Burns plant was closed under orders on February 19. In short, I think it will be apparent that there were seven days between the time it was reported that the disease was taking on a more serious turn and the time it was established as foot-and-mouth disease.
I think I should say-although it is not in this record; I had it over the phone and otherwise just before coming to the house-that the material upon which there was proof of foot-and-mouth disease in the area was taken from three animals, I think it was, in the Burns plant. That is, these materials were not taken elsewhere. The evidence with regard to the other cases would indicate that it may have been stomatitis that was on these different farms that I am going to refer to in a moment; or there is a possibility that on some of them it may have been foot-and-mouth disease, but there is no absolute proof with regard to that.
The material taken in order to have the tests made at Ottawa was taken from three animals, perhaps I should not say in the Bums plant, but in the Burns feed lot, where animals remain for some time and are fed before they are slaughtered. I understand these animals were from among those, and the tests were made, and they were found to be suffering from some disease. The samples were taken there, and the tests were made in Ottawa.

speechtext: Where did these three animals come from?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Can I get that information?

speechtext: They should be able to give it.

The assurance is that they were traced right through to wherever they

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

speechtext:
After we are through with it here, yes.
I believe I have given most of the information asked for last night, if not all of it. If there are any other inquiries, I would say that I have with me my three officials who are closest to the whole matter, and they will be able to give me answers to any questions which may be asked in this connection.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Were precautions taken to find out exactly from what farms those three cattle came to the Burns feed lot?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
My information is that there were about eighty animals in this feed lot. It would require very close examination of all the records back for a number of weeks, and possibly extending into months. I think hon. members understand what a feed lot is, associated with a packing plant. The animals are brought in, but some of them are not fit for slaughter. They are fed and brought to the point where they can be slaughtered. Sometimes it takes weeks, and sometimes it may run into a couple of months. However, it was three of those animals. Up to the present time I am not in a position, and neither is any other person, to state exactly where those three animals came from. An effort has been made to trace them.

We have had no evidence even yet, Mr. Chairman, to show that gross negligence has not existed in the detection of this dread disease that is so vital to the livestock industry of this country, and which will in turn affect every Canadian citizen.
The events as we have had them given to us were that on November 26 a suspicious disease condition in cattle was reported to a private veterinarian. On December 2, two dominion government veterinarians visited the farm and placed it under at least partial quarantine. We are told that on December 3, two horses were inoculated. Obviously those two government veterinarians placed that farm under quarantine because they were suspicious of some other disease. On December 7 the Ottawa office was notified of this disease, but it was not until January 15 that the veterinary director general visited the area. According to the minister's report of yesterday he was suspicious of foot-and-mouth disease being present at the Bums packing plant or Burns feed lot.
The minister says that only two animals have gone out of that yard and that approximately 78 were shot. As I understand it, they were not shot until March 2, and were kept at the Burns yard from January 17 until March 2. The first full inoculation procedure took place on February 16 at the animal diseases research institute in Hull. May I ask who arranged for that material to be sent down to Hull? Obviously the veterinary director general had changed his mind sufficiently to leave Ottawa for that infected area, and peculiarly enough on the same day these animals were injected. He issued quarantine instructions on February 17, although the results of the animal inoculation in Hull were not available until February 24.
Now, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that something is wrong. Why did the veterinary director general not leave until the 16th, the

Foot-and-mouth disease day those animals were inoculated at Hull? Why did he proceed with quarantine the very next day on his arrival at the area? Was it because he was afraid that there might be foot-and-mouth disease in the area or was he satisfied in his own mind that it was already there? Whether we like it or not the competence of those now responsible for the services providing protection against such a calamity is undoubtedly in question.

So long as even a suspicion existed that this could be foot-and-mouth disease, it was the responsibility of the head of the health of animals branch to ascertain positively, and at the earliest possible moment, whether it was or was not this dreaded disease. I should like to ask the minister for an explanation of the government's policy regarding the slaughtering of these animals. If I understood! him correctly many of these cattle are being slaughtered today and, so far as the government knows, they have not foot-and-mouth disease but have been exposed in one way or another to the disease. I take it I am right thus far. If that is the case, the cattle have a clear bill of health and, so far as the government knows, show no signs of having the disease. Why could these cattle not be segregated and placed under a very rigorous quarantine within the greater quarantine area, held there for three months, and if they are still given a clear bill of health surely there will be no need to slaughter them.
What is the policy in regard to the importation into Canada of cattle from countries where foot-and mouth disease is prevalent? For example, in England foot-and-mouth disease has been present for a long time. I have some personal knowledge of this. Supposing a person buys cattle in England, and between the time he buys those cattle and has them shipped into quarantine in Scotland foot-and-mouth disease breaks out near by. What happens? Those cattle are quarantined within that district for a period of three months!. If at the end of three months they

can be given a clean bill of health, then they are exported to Scotland where they are quarantined for another three months. If at the end of that time they still do not have foot-and-mouth disease, they are shipped to Canada. Upon arrival in Canada, they are again placed in quarantine for another three months. At the end of that three months they are tested and, if they are still clear of the disease, they are shipped to the farmer.
Why cannot some similar procedure be adopted in this case? If tests show these cattle to be free of foot-and-mouth disease today but they have been exposed to infection, why could they not be segregated and placed under rigorous quarantine within the greater quarantine area? If these cattle were all common beef cattle, perhaps I would not raise the point; but I understand many of these cattle are valuable. You cannot compute their value in dollars. They represent generations of work in breeding stock. It seems to me we are today slaughtering cattle that have not got foot-and-mouth disease but may have been exposed to it. I would have thought it would have been possible to impose a rigorous quarantine and save some of those animals.

There are not any such

Why are you killing them

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: We are not killing them. The only place we are killing animals is inside the quarantined area, and that is just an area around Regina extending about twenty-five miles in each direction. That is the area where the animals are being killed.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Are you going to kill them all?

speechtext:
Then we add another thirty miles approximately on the average, fifty

miles from the nearest cases where animals have had the disease, and we call that a buffer area; and we say we will not ship those animals to anybody to be further fed and so on, or even ship them into other areas, except to get them to a plant where they can be immediately slaughtered. That is exactly what is done over in Scotland and elsewhere.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Yes, but you are talking about cattle within the quarantined area. You say that as far as you know those cattle outside of the quarantined area have not got foot-and-mouth disease.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I will come back to that
matter in a minute. Let us get this other one clear. That means that all of western Canada, so far as anybody knows, is absolutely clear of foot-and-mouth disease at this moment except this area that is fifty miles square just around Regina.
To come back to my hon. friend's question, we have not done anything to prevent animals from being shipped out of the remaining area; but some of our provinces unfortunately have done so. It has been said by some of them that you cannot ship cattle through here or there; that is as to cattle as to which there is not any more chance of their having foot-and-mouth disease now than there was a year ago.
Then we have just this morning been told that you cannot ship cattle across a province in order to bring them from two of the western provinces to eastern Canada. It is from those provinces that most of the cattle will have to come if they come for slaughter and also from them that most of the hogs that are surplus will have to come. We are told: You cannot ship them across there. It is all very well to say to us what we should do, but that is the position taken up to date.
Going back into the area the question is asked: Why do you slaughter them? The first reason is that if we did not slaughter them, there is not a chance in the world of our getting back into the United States market. That is the practice that is followed in the United States and it is the practice that they believe ought to be followed. Our effort in what we are doing is to get back into that market as soon as we can and we are following the same practice that they follow. It is one thing to say that they do this other thing in Britain and do something else on the continent. They have had the disease for gen-jrations on the continent of Europe and for a long time in Britain. I am told in most of those countries they do not do what we do. One of the reasons they do -not do it is on account of what I mentioned last night,
Foot-and-mouth disease namely, that there is no danger in eating that meat. There is no danger to a human being in eating the meat. In countries where they require the meat and cannot afford to buy it, they use the meat.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: They cook it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: They cook it and put it in cans, or cure it or do something else with it, and use it. But we are here living on a continent where it has been the practice, not only in the United States but in this country, to keep foot-and-mouth disease out of these two areas. Therefore the practice has been followed in the United States right up until now-we have never had to follow it until now-of killing all animals that come in contact with the disease. If we are going to get back into the United States market at any reasonable time in the future, we shall have to follow that policy. There will be a certain amount of doubt. Even -as to animals that we might think bad foot-and-mouth disease we will do it. But from listening to the arguments put forward here, I am sure that many of the members in the house are far more fully convinced than I am that -all those animals had foot-and-mouth disease. They being so convinced, you -can quite understand how other people would feel if those animals are allowed, within the next six months or a year, to come out of those areas and be shipped into other parts of Canada. So we say the better thing to do is to slaughter all of them that have come in contact with the disease, thus absolutely removing any possibility of marketing them. Thus we can say not only to other parts of Canada but to the United States: There is not any danger whatsoever in your taking animals out of the western part of Canada and using them as feeders or for any other purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
May I be permitted to say a word or two, Mr. Chairman? It may possibly be on account of my unusual ability that eight speakers are permitted on the other side to one on this side in connection with this matter. There is one thing on which I disagree with the Minister of Agriculture, although I do not disagree with him entirely. He says they are not slaughtering any animals at the present time. I know of one old cow that died after walking from Middlesex East because I had part of it for lunch in the restaurant upstairs. I quite agree with the hon. member for Calgary West in what he said yesterday. The reason I am saying that -and it is not a matter of levity-is that there has unquestionably been entertained among some the opinion that it is not safe to eat the meat. As far as I am concerned, the hon. member for Calgary West can send me all the meat he likes-that is not alive-into British

Foot-and-mouth disease Columbia; he can fill my locker from his farm any time he likes and I will advertise that I have that meat there.
When I took part in this discussion on the day after the house opened, I said I did not think there was any use of talking about past mistakes or what has happened. I have been in accord with most of what has been said in this house. I am sorry to say that one or two have tried to make political capital out of the situation. I am sorry for that. During a war we must govern ourselves accordingly for the best interest of Canada. I believe this is a war; it is a war to defend our country with respect to agriculture and I believe that means the economy of Canada as a whole. For that reason I think we should look at the matter from a non-partisan point of view. The discussion on the first day was taken up with consideration of what would be paid to the farmers for the loss of their cattle, and other compensation. I take the stand that this is a national calamity. I want to mention to you three national calamities that we have had in the Dominion of Canada-and I use the word "dominion". The three national calamities were the floods in British Columbia; the Red river flood; and the Rimouski fire. What happened? This parliament was most generous and most fair to the people of those districts affected. That policy was endorsed by the people of Canada. I believe that this parliament will be most fair and most generous to the farmers who, unfortunately, lose any stock through this tragedy which we are now experiencing.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Parliament or the government.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Parliament. Parliament is supreme, and this government has at all times recognized the fact that parliament is supreme. I believe that if this parliament did not do so of its own accord, the people of Canada would see to it that we acted in a fair and generous manner in this calamity which is facing us at the present time.
I am sorry to say that all too many of my colleagues do not view this matter with the seriousness with which I view it. As I said on the second day of this session, and I will repeat it now, this is the most important legislation that will face us at this session. Fortunately, to date, the outbreak has not been severe; just a small area has been affected. I feel extremely sorry for those farmers. I am sorry their names were mentioned in the first place. But this is a war. It is a war to eradicate this disease. Whenever you have a war, unfortunately some people must suffer. I am sure they are worthy citizens and good farmers, and they have my entire sympathy.

I happen to represent a district that produces milk. I do not represent a beef country. I represent a district that produces 75 per cent, on a conservative estimate, of all the fluid milk used in the province of British Columbia. I am naturally concerned about those farmers. I am not worried about the absolutely ridiculous way, as I see it, that this affair was carried on in the first place. Unfortunately-and I repeat it, whether the minister likes it or not-we have some officials who should not be in positions they hold now. But fortunately there is a job waiting for them to which they can be transferred without loss of prestige and which they are more capable of doing, namely digging the St. Lawrence waterway with a shovel. I have no apology for making that statement. We have veterinarians in the Dominion of Canada, we have them in British Columbia and in my own riding, who are capable, but we have some very inefficient ones in high positions in the Department of Agriculture right in Ottawa. I know what I would do with them if I were Minister of Agriculture. It is now four-thirty. By seven minutes to five, if that were long enough, they would be gone. I have nothing more to say about that.
What is the use of worrying about what has happened in the past? Let us look to the future. It was emphasized the other day, and I am sure the Minister of Agriculture will emphasize it, that the greatest loss we have had is the loss of the United States market. I understand the embargo is on for sixty days. Incidentally, Mr. Chairman, for the benefit of Hansard and my own constituency, I want you to note that I am not reading my speech or even speaking from notes. I have never done that and never will. If I have to do that I shall do like others, give a copy of it to the press gallery and to Hansard before I deliver it. As I have said, the greatest loss we have had so far is the loss of the United States market. I know nothing about American politics but I have lived long enough to take an even bet that the embargo will be on until at least November of this year, and for certain reasons. I believe the embargo will be on for a long long time.
This is the fourth calamity that has struck the country in recent years, as was mentioned in the house yesterday by the Minister of Agriculture. The first was the Fraser river flood, the second was the Red river flood and the third the Rimouski fire. I want to point out to you what they did at the time of the Red river flood, Mr. Chairman. I say this for the benefit of some hon. members who represent rural ridings in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, who look upon this

matter as just taking up time. I want to point out to you what they did in Manitoba and in the city of Winnipeg at the time of the Red river flood.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: What has that to do with foot-and-mouth disease?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
They went out and got the best available engineers who had recent experience to advise them on floods. I hope that satisfies my hon. friend who interrupted me. If you know what is coming you will not interrupt, but I do not think you will ever see that far. They got the best engineers they could find who had had experience in floods to advise them. What happened with respect to rehabilitation? They brought in two men from British Columbia who had assisted in rehabilitation after the floods in the Fraser valley in 1948. I am very proud of the fact that the Manitoba government wired the government of British Columbia asking for these men, and they were flown in immediately. I refer to Colonel Baldwin and Mr. W. L. Mackin, who happened to come from my riding. They stayed in Winnipeg as long as the Manitoba government desired to have them there to advise on rehabilitation. 1 mention that, Mr. Chairman, to indicate what the federal government should do because unquestionably some of their officials have fallen down. That is a thing of the past. They did not have the knowledge. I do not think they have the experience. I will leave it at that, because that is the kindest way I can put it.
If I were the Minister of Agriculture I would go to the United States and I would ask them to lend me a competent man. They have had experience with this disease. I would ask them to lend me the finest veterinarians they have. I would go to Holland, to Britain and to other parts of Europe, and I would ask for the loan of those veterinarians who have had experience in this disease. I would have them brought in here. I am sure these governments would send them to us as a friendly act under the Colombo plan or reverse lend-lease, if you like. In addition, Mr. Chairman, we have numerous planes that are flying abroad on what I would call joy trips; they are flying certain people all over the world. We could send a few of them to pick up these veterinarians who have had experience.
As the minister says, I believe this terrible disease has been confined to a small area. I believe it has not cost the country or the individual farmers a very great deal up to the present time, but our biggest loss is the United States market. How can we possibly get the United States people to lift the embargo at an early date? The only way that I can see we can do it is to do as I
Foot-and-mouth disease suggest, namely, bring in veterinarians from Europe who have had experience, and also veterinarians from Mexico and Britain. If we do that we will go a long way toward gaining the good will of the United States congress and we will show them that we are not dependent on our local officials but are willing to call on those who have experience, which has been exemplified by their past efforts. Speaking on behalf of my riding-in spite of the fact that a great many of my colleagues do not see it as I do, I view it as the most serious thing facing our country today. It is the first thing that the government should take into consideration and I earnestly urge the minister to consult with some of these countries through his officials. I would like to see done exactly what was done at the time of the Fraser valley flood. At that time the Minister of Trade and Commerce sent a capable engineer to British Columbia. I would like to see these experienced veterinarians come here, if for no other reason than to convince the American people that we are sincere in our endeavour to eradicate the disease so that we may have the embargo lifted.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: May I just say a word? The only thing I wish to reply to is the suggestion of bringing in veterinarians. We have already done what the hon. member has suggested in so far as the United States are concerned. They sent up Dr. Shahan, who is the top United States authority, and the man who conducted this campaign in Mexico against foot-and-mouth disease. He does not remain there constantly, but he is in and out of the district, advising our people and assisting them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: What about these experts from European countries? Could we not bring in some of them? I am sure the governments would send them over if we asked for them.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Our feeling with regard to that is that their objective in these countries is so different from our objective here that it is better to depend upon the United States advice. Our objective is the same as that of the United States, namely, to destroy it entirely in the small area, and we are using the best men we have here and the best men the United States can send us.

speechtext:
I should like to ask a question about the inability of the Burns company to tell the department where the cattle came from. It may well be so and yet I doubt it. It is certainly most important that the department ascertain as far as possible where the company bought these cattle. My hon. friend, the

Foot-and-mouth disease member for Selkirk, tells me that when he delivers cattle to the stockyards he gets a cheque for the cattle delivered. Can the department not find out from Bums what cheques they made out, and to whom, during this period we are discussing, in an endeavour to find out at least the individuals who sold cattle to Burns, and then to check, through those individuals, where they bought or received their cattle from. Surely the Burns company is willing to co-operate with the department to that extent. Can the minister give us any information about that?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
1 cannot add very much to the information I have already given on it, that I do not think there is any hesitation on the part of Burns to give us all the information they can. There is no doubt that we have done everything we could in order to get all the information they have. But what they tell us is-and we think there is some reason in it-that if you turn 80 cattle into a feed lot and you send one of your employees in from day to day in order to pick out those which are ready to slaughter and drive them into a slaughter house and have them slaughtered, unless he has kept a very careful record of each animal he takes today and where they came from, it would not be very long until it would be difficult for anyone to say that this animal came from that farm. If the Burns company did say that the animal came off a farm where there never had been any of the disease, I should think the individual who had been named might feel that he had some right of action in the matter.
There is no doubt they will be careful. I am sure that as soon as they can give us the information, they will give it to us, if they can.	[DOT]

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Are they branded cattle?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: No, they are not branded. Well, perhaps I should not say they are not, because some of them might be. Some might come off the small ranches south of Regina, where they do use brands.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I can see
the difficulty in tracing cattle. However, this matter is so serious that every possible check should be made as to the conditions on farms of those who delivered cattle to Burns and Company during this time. One way of doing it would be to go through their records and finding out those to whom they paid cheques.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I should like to come to the defence of the packing plants. Some hon. members say that these tickets are issued. I ship millions of dollars' worth


of stock to the Burns plant and I can say here without the shadow of a doubt that that is their living, their livelihood. That is what they will try to do and, I am sure, what they are trying to do. They will try to get to the bottom of this so as to find out exactly where these cattle came from.
These buyers go to the stockyards and proceed in a fashion different from that followed in eastern Canada. They might have ten or a dozen killers. In that pen there might be one that is generally known as a sixty. That is what the buyer goes by, and that pen is put on the ticket. The animal goes to the weight scale and is weighed. Then it goes to the feed lot. The only man who could pick it out of the feed lot is the man who raised it.
Burns have a double duty. The first duty is to protect the man who shipped the steer, and to be absolutely sure that it did come from that farm. His neighbour might say that the farm is infected with foot-and-mouth disease. If Burns and Company were wrong, it would be a bad thing for the farmer. Burns cannot afford to be wrong.
Why do hon. members say that Burns and Company are shirking their duty, and that they are not trying to find out where the animals came from? I say that Burns will do everything they can to produce that ticket to show where the animal came from, just as soon as they are absolutely sure.
I have been in the cattle business ever since I was knee high to a grasshopper and, during that time, I have been through glanders epidemics. I have been through what we called cattle mange when we dipped all the cattle in an area thirty miles around. I have complete faith in the officials in the Department of Agriculture, and in the provincial officials, and I am sure they will clean up this mess. Let us be fair to the farmer. Let us be fair to all those people out in Saskatchewan. Let us forget all this discussion and get down to passing the bill. Let us help those boys out there on the farms who are suffering right now.

speechtext: How long will the quarantine of this area be kept up?

speechtext: I was about to correct the suggestion of the hon. member for Fraser Valley when he said it would be sixty days. There is no limit on the quarantine. The quarantine is on. Under American law it cannot be taken off until sixty days after the department of agriculture in the United States is satisfied that we have eradicated the disease. Their regulations provide that they cannot take the quarantine off this country until they are sure the disease has been eradicated.

speechtext: I think the minister has misunderstood my question. He is now referring to the embargo. The United States has nothing to do with the quarantining of our cattle.

Well, an embargo with
respect to this country is a quarantine in this country, so long as the foot-and-mouth disease is here. We cannot send animals out.

speechtext: I do not know that I should say anything more than I have said, namely, that I think we would find it necessary, not only in order to satisfy the United States but in order to satisfy people in other parts of Canada that we are going to keep the district closed, to say that we will apply practically the same regulation as the Americans apply. That regulation is that, once they are satisfied the area has been cleaned up, then they believe they should keep the embargo on for at least another sixty days.

It is an embargo against us, so far as they are concerned. Their law says that they must place an embargo against the shipment of livestock into the United States from any country in which there is foot-and-mouth disease. Then their regulations go on to say that they cannot take that off until sixty days after the department of agriculture in that country is satisfied that the disease has been cleaned up. We will have to satisfy the people in other parts of Canada that we have taken the same care with regard to this quarantined district. Otherwise they will have reason to complain, if we begin to ship earlier.

speechtext: From the minister's statement this afternoon, and from what he now says- and I hope he will correct me if I am wrong- it seems to me that the quarantined area, about 2,500 square miles in extent, is likely to remain in a state of quarantine for quite a few months-or, as the minister himself said, perhaps six months or a year. subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

We are hopeful that we may be able to clean up this area in a much shorter time than three months, say. We may be wrong in that. Then for some period after that we would have to keep control.

It will take the department here at least a few months to clean up the situation. Then we will have whatever further period the United States will insist on. There may be a minimum quarantine period within that area of five or six months. Let us just have a look at the way this quarantine is going to affect, not only the twenty or thirty farmers on whose farms the disease now exists but the two thousand other farmers in this area.
A ban has been placed on the movement of grain. A lot of this grain is in a damp condition. Thousands and thousands of bushels of damp grain are in the country elevators in that area or on the farms themselves. Spring is just around the corner and then we will have a period when heating and spoilage of damp grain will occur. These farmers who have damp grain may lose because of this quarantine just as surely as those farmers whose cattle are affected.
I want to know from the minister what the	government	will	do	to	assist	those
farmers whose cattle are affected.
I want to know from the minister what the	government	will	do	to	assist	those
farmers who have damp grain which may spoil because of the quarantine. There are many farmers in that area with the bulk of their 1951 crops still on the farm or out in the field. How will they be able to farm this year with a ban on the shipment of grain when many of the elevators are plugged

with grain at the present moment? What consideration will the government give to providing some income stability for those farmers or some compensation for the spoilage of damp grain?
What about the producers of milk within the area whose cattle may be slaughtered? They will receive compensation for their capital investment in cattle, but under the legislation as it is now drafted they will not get any compensation for loss of revenue through inability to produce milk for the next year or so.

The disease was diagnosed as stomatitis. That was in December, and by January 6 they were clear of any disease. It is impossible to go and test those cattle. I have sat here since
yesterday afternoon, Mr. Chairman, listening with great interest to this debate. I must say that before I came here my only knowledge of this difficulty was from reading press reports. Since this debate commenced, I have learned a lot. I want to say that, like many other members, I particularly appreciated the explanation of this disease given to the house by the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth. I thought he enlightened us to a great extent, particularly in view of the fact that the minister had previously left the impression that one had to send to England to obtain some material in order to diagnose the disease.
After listening carefully to the debate I have come to the conclusion that there has been gross negligence on the part of the members of the health of animals branch. I believe that in this case some of the minister's senior officials have let him down very badly. I was surprised, after the debate had progressed to the point it had, that the minister made such a vigorous defence of his officials without obtaining more information. It was obvious to me that the minister was not very well informed on the actual situation when this debate began.
In view of the fact that the director general of veterinary services has viewed this subject with great alarm in reports given to this house throughout the years, I am surprised at the delay in dealing with the matter. To

Foot-and-mouth disease indicate the concern of the director general I am going to read a short paragraph or two of the annual report from the veterinary director general, T. Childs, V.S., D.V.M. In his annual report for the year ending March 31, 1950, dealing with this question, he said:
As the danger of foot-and-mouth disease being introduced into Canada from countries where this disease is permitted to exist is always present, and has been enhanced during recent years by the ease and rapidity with which transportation may be effected by air, the presence of this disease in countries with which Canada has trade relations is a matter of deep concern. In this connection it is reassuring to note that foot-and-mouth disease, which appeared in the republic of Mexico during 1946, and spread over wide areas of that country before effective measures could be taken to control it, has, through the joint efforts of Mexican and United States authorities, been brought under control. However, as there are but a few countries in the world which are known to be entirely free of this disease, it is imperative that the greatest vigilance be exercised at all times to prevent this disease from being introduced into Canada by regular trade channels.
The director general says the greatest vigilance is necessary. After listening to this debate, Mr. Chairman, I am quite sure that no one could truthfully say that the greatest vigilance had been exercised so far as the outbreak of this disease is concerned. Now I want to read another short paragraph in that report:
Uncooked, chilled, or frozen meats, or meat food products from countries where the disease exists are particularly dangerous and no products of this nature are accepted for entry to Canada.
At that point I want to suggest that if seven veterinary officials from the director general's department made seven negative reports, surely that fact alone should be sufficient to arouse suspicion. The very fact that seven were called in indicates some element of doubt in the minds of those who were investigating the question. In my opinion, where there was any element of doubt, extra vigilance should have been exercised.
Now I want to read from the report of the veterinary director general for the year ended March 31, 1951. This is what he has to say at page 6:
The danger of foot-and-mouth disease being introduced into Canada through normal trade activities, or otherwise, from countries in which this destructive disease is permitted to exist, continues to be a matter of serious concern. This disease has never gained a foothold in Canada, consequently Canadian livestock, that is, cattle, other ruminants and swine, can be considered as being decidedly vulnerable. Therefore, the introduction of this disease into Canada would likely be attended by greater than average mortality, and greater than average impairment of productive capacity of infected animals, if such animals were permitted to survive. It is noted with satisfaction and considerable relief, that the foot-and-mouth disease situation in Mexico appears to be very well in hand.

Then the report goes on to deal at further length with this disease. In view of the fact that the director general admits the greater hazards owing to the rapidity of air transportation and, I presume, of immigration and that sort of thing, I would have thought that he would have advised his minister to recommend to the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration that special precautions should be taken with respect to immigrants coming from infected areas in European countries. The very fact that this was not done-and it is a practice in other countries-in my opinion indicates further negligence in dealing with this most serious question.
I do not intend to speak for long, Mr. Chairman. This is not the first instance, in my opinion, and that of a good many people who are interested in agriculture and of scientific agriculturists, which indicates that the department of the director general is not functioning as it should function today in the interests of agriculture. I refer to Newcastle disease in poultry, as to which there has been a great deal of experience in the United States. A great deal of work has been undertaken in Great Britain. Yet the director general insisted on a policy of slaughtering hundreds of thousands of poultry, and paying compensation, in an effort to stamp out the disease. It is a fact that this year the policy is changed, and there is now in effect a policy of mass vaccination by live vaccine of poultry in this country. This has been the situation regardless of the fact that a good many animal pathologists in Canada and in other countries were not in favour of the previous policy, as the result of years of study. I say frankly, Mr. Chairman, that there are a good number of people in this country interested in scientific agriculture who are of the opinion that there is not the best of co-operation between various branches of the minister's department, such as between the department of the director general and the various laboratories, the director general is inclined to be living in the horse-and-buggy days, as one prominent agriculturist said to me two days ago, and that it is exceedingly difficult to get him out of the ruts of those days. I have talked to qualified pathologists in Canada, and I have talked to one or two qualified United States pathologists; and I listened to those people with a great deal of interest. They were quite critical of certain aspects of our administration so far as the director general's branch is concerned.
I suggest that the minister would be well advised to go thoroughly into all aspects of this question and inquire into the operation of this branch of the department. I was

pleased to see the minister and his fellow ministers who were with him in the house at the time quite readily agreed that this matter should be the subject of investigation by the committee on agriculture. In view of the experience of Canadian poultry producers in connection with Newcastle disease and in view of this outbreak, I suggest that the question to be discussed by the standing committee on agriculture should be an investigation into the health of animals branch of the minister's department.

The other thing I wish to comment on is this. My hon. friend said he did not know anything about this matter when we started discussing it.

He apparently learned somewhere-either in the press or in the debate in this house-something different. He is therefore critical. I have here the statement which was made the other day by Dr. M. S. Shahan, chief of the United States animal industry virus research board. It was made in a speech at 55704-8
Foot-and-mouth disease Regina on Wednesday of last week. The report is dated February 28. Here is what he says about the matter:
Speaking of the American livestock embargo, Dr. Shahan said that it would not be lifted until freedom from the disease has been determined by the Canadian officials and the U.S. government is confident of the conclusion. "It depends upon how quickly the disease is eradicated."
Dr. Shahan denied earlier reports that there was a trainload of foot-and-mouth vaccine in Chicago ready to be moved to any point of contamination which may appear in the U.S. "We have no foot-and-mouth vaccine in the U.S.," the American virus-diseases expert said. There is a question which I am not competent to discuss. It has to do with what is called the war by means of viruses or by means of different methods of distributing disease. There are standing international regulations as to whose workings even I am denied full knowledge as is any other member of this house. These regulations do exist, and it is under these regulations that we must go to Britain to get the serum that is necessary in order to deal with this matter in its final stages. It is all very well to say that an ordinary veterinarian practising around the country can come to the conclusion that this is stomatitis, and everybody accepts his opinion. But eventually you get to the point where there is some reason for thinking otherwise and the only way that you can finally nail the thing down is by getting the serum from the proper place, and it was obtained from the only place we could obtain it.

The minister at least told the hon. member for Calgary East that all of the animals that were sold and disposed of by Burns had been identified and found to be free of disease. That being so, the lack of knowledge he displayed earlier today has been changed by the information that he has obtained recently, or within the last few hours, which shows, according to his statement, that each of these animals has been properly followed and found not to be a carrier of or to suffer from the disease.
Having said that, one does not want in any way to place before the committee information, however dependable, unless he can vouch for the facts. That is the course I have always followed, and for that reason I welcomed the minister's undertaking yesterday that the committee on agriculture would

Foot-and-mouth disease in fact be set up. I take it that this Committee will be set up immediately, because unless it is it will-

As the Minister of Finance says, it is a standing committee, and I presume it will be convened immediately so that all information may be forthcoming and we will have an opportunity of examining the deputy minister and the officials of the department in order to secure the information that should have been procured from the packers and also generally in connection with the matter.
I want to make it clear that parliament holds governments responsible, not civil servants, and no official of a department should in any way be held responsible for what has been termed the gross negligence that is more apparent as the minister answers. That responsibility is not discharged by making a scapegoat of any official of the government, because the government must accept the responsibility for the failure of those departments over which it has authority.
I was impressed by what the hon. member for Assiniboia said. He raised most clearly and fairly the situation that prevails in this area of some 2,500 square miles, and the great difficulties that the farmers are going to have because of their inability to dispose of their crops, and also from the fact, as he pointed out, and properly so, that the elevators there are in the same position as elevators generally throughout the province, namely, packed with damp or tough grain, and therefore making it all the more difficult to dispose of.
I raised that question yesterday and I went on to deal with the subject matter of this legislation. The hon. member for Assiniboia asked the minister some questions yesterday regarding the meaning of section 2(1). If I understood the minister aright, he interpreted section 2(1) to mean that in addition to what is provided as payment under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act there would be paid a further amount, namely, an amount which is fair and reasonable, as determined by the valuation board. If I am correct in my understanding of what the minister said yesterday, then what is provided here is in addition to the $40, or the $100, as the case may be, that is provided in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. I think the hon. member for Fort William was right when he said it was legislation, that was so drawn that everybody could understand it. My understanding

of section 2(1) is that it does not so provide. The wording is:
Notwithstanding anything in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, the Minister of Agriculture may order that fair and reasonable compensation be paid . . .
I do not think the word "notwithstanding" should be there. In order to clarify it, it should provide that: "In addition to anything provided for in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act ..." I am passing this on to the minister because I think that parliament wants to draft legislation that will mean what the minister and parliament intend it shall mean. I suggest for his consideration that the word "notwithstanding" be deleted, and that there be substituted therefor:
In addition to any payment provided for in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, the Minister of Agriculture may order that fair and reasonable compensation be paid1 . . .
And so forth. That would remove any misunderstanding so that farmers generally would know exactly that what they are going to receive is in addition to what is provided for in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
Yesterday I asked the minister whether "fair and reasonable compensation" was not in fact a term which generally leaves to the valuation board or to the minister and the governor in council power to determine without a yardstick, which no legislation should permit. I brought this to the minister's attention and pointed out that certain cattle will have their commercial value, and the minister agreed with it, and other purebred cattle will have a very much greater value. The minister also indicated that some cows will be with calf, and that allowances should be made in such a case. Today the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out the potential loss, for reasons beyond their control, that will be occasioned to dairy farmers who will be denied their livelihood not only during the period of the quarantine but possibly a good deal longer and until such time as they are able to restore their herds. What I had in mind yesterday was that we in parliament must make legislation effectual so as to afford insurance against the loss by these farmers of these intangibles such as have been referred to by the minister and also by the hon. member for Assiniboia. I take it, from what the minister said, that he felt keenly the difficulties that are bound to arise, having regard to the embargoes that are being brought into existence by the provinces. There is one thing however against which we in Canada must guard, and that is the possibility of the balkanization of Canada.
Carried to the limits that would appear to be constitutionally possible today, we would be doing in effect what the fathers of confederation never hoped or expected, in that we would be bringing about the creation of superior jurisdictions in the relations between one province and another.

However, if Your Honour rules that, even having regard to the extraordinary conditions *that prevail, the sections should not be referred to particularly, then I shall of course restrict myself to a discussion of what should be in the bill, while generally accepting the principle of the bill.
What I want to bring to the attention of the house particularly is that we join with hon. members in all parts of the house in accepting the principle of this bill. The need for expeditious action in order to meet a situation which all of us regard as most serious to the agricultural economy, and indeed the prosperity of all Canadians, is evident. The situation in the restricted area in the province of Saskatchewan requires that compensation should be paid to those who are suffering by reason of the visitation of this malady which caused damage to these people beyond anything that any of us would have contemplated a few short months ago. In arriving at a basis for compensation, my submission is that the basis should be the ordinary allowances that are provided for under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, plus something that will assure, to the farmers affected, compensation to meet those intangible losses which are difficult to cover in a statute.
Many of these farmers have built up their dairy herds, and this is particularly so having regard to the fact that the area under quarantine surrounds the city of Regina, and now find themselves in a position where not only their herds are going to be destroyed but probably their livelihood for a considerable period of time. What I have in mind is that this emergency calls for compensation to cover not only the economic value of the animals that are destroyed, but also those intangibles that were mentioned by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) in the committee on the resolution, such as the prospective progeny of the animal destroyed and also an allowance in respect of the loss of income which will arise to those in the area. Many of these farmers face the future

with fear, their herds either destroyed or under a potential sentence of destruction. They ask parliament not for a handout, not for anything in the nature of charity, but for compensation for the loss which they will suffer which is more than the value of the animals in question. I feel that in the legislation there should be incorporated some provision for a yardstick which will assure that reasonable compensation without which the legislation will be ineffectual to meet the situation that prevails.
I am not going to discuss all the other matters to which reference has been made, except to say that when provision is made in the bill for compensation to those who have any buildings, fodder or grains destroyed, there should be some basis to assure that the compensation will meet the exigencies which have arisen by reason of this calamity that has struck the area. The people there face the future, not hopelessly but fearfully. They realize that they have nothing to look forward to so far as their farm operations are concerned for months ahead. They ask that, in the interpretation of the basis upon which they are to receive compensation, the spirit of their loss rather than 'the letter of the law, strictly enforced, shall form the basis for that payment.
I feel that parliament has done itself proud in the manner in which it has approached this problem. Sometimes parliament is condemned because it is ineffectual and fails to represent or spearhead the wish and desire of the nation. In the past two days, in the course of questioning and discussion, facts have been elucidated; circumstances have been reviewed; and members in all parts of this house have endeavoured to represent what parliament should normally represent, the will of the people. Speaking as one from a constituency in which part of this affected area is located, and speaking for the members from the western provinces and for my own province in particular, I say that each and every one of us in the province of Saskatchewan appreciates that feeling of fellowship and co-operation that has been evident here. We know that out of this legislation will come a new hope to the people in the areas stricken by a pestilence which is well-nigh indescribable. To the members of this house from every part of Canada, on behalf of those within that area who today are suffering from a cause over which they have no control, I know I express the sentiments of the people of the province of Saskatchewan when I say "Thank you."

If the herd is destroyed and the farmers are compensated for their loss and taxed under the ordinary set-up today they will be paying much more than they should, and that would make it much more difficult for those who wish to start in the same line of business again. It is important that consideration be given to that matter.
I am sorry at this time that other provision has not been made to guarantee the future of this great cattle industry in some way. I listened to the news broadcast at six o'clock tonight and I heard that in my own province one-third of the employees of the great packing industry in that province have received notice that they will be laid off. I must say that I was a bit surprised at the action taken yesterday by the government of my own province. Probably they have felt that they were forced into it, because I understood they were going to co-operate very closely with the federal authorities; but when they were questioned yesterday on their announcement, the provincial minister of agriculture said that they had decided to act on their own to protect the province of Manitoba and the producers there. I understand that British Columbia produces about
10 per cent of the meat that is normally consumed in that province. In a few days, in this great country, there will develop a situation such as I never dreamed could happen under any consideration whatever. As I see it, we are now going to have a different set of prices in the different provinces of this country for beef and meats, depending on the production within those provinces. I never imagined that the various provinces would place embargoes to the extent that they have done. It will create difficulties. Some provinces that have a great surplus of meat production will be in this position. The producers of those provinces in all likelihood will not receive the average price that they would if we had the understanding throughout this dominion that we should have. On the other hand, in other provinces where the shortage exists the consumers will probably be forced to pay a great deal more for the meat than they should pay. Therefore I hope that the minister or the federal government will take some means of consulting, or having a meeting, with those provincial representatives as soon as possible to bring about a common understanding in the interests of both the meat producers and the consumers of this great nation of ours.
It is very important. I know this thing has happened in a hurry. That meeting should be held as soon as possible. Again I return to this great cattle industry into which many people have put their life savings. The strides in development that have been made in purebred herds in this country in the past few years have been astonishing. These people are discouraged today. This is not only a severe blow to the agricultural industry of this country, but it will affect the entire economy of the nation, because agriculture, apart from beef production, had been slipping pretty fast in the past few months. The income in other branches of agriculture has been dropping while the cost of production has been increasing consistently. According to the federal bureau of statistics, they estimate an increase of at least 5 per cent or more in the general cost of production on the farms this year, but when you think of the whole picture and that the one branch of agriculture where there was some revenue left, and which many farmers were using in order to carry on the other operations of their farms, was the cattle industry, and when you see that jeopardized to the extent it has been today, you have some idea of the extremely difficult position in which it places agriculture almost overnight. Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words on the second reading of this bill. My colleague the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright) has just placed our views before the house. We are happy to support the bill; we are happy to support the amendment suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker); and we would like to see the bill extended so that all those who suffered loss on account of action made necessary by the disease in the area affected will receive compensation.
But the point that was raised by the hon. member for Souris (Mr. Ross) should be pressed upon the government and the government should take note of it, namely, the serious result to the two provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan on account of the embargoes imposed by the neighbouring provinces on the passage of livestock, meat and so on through their provinces and emphasized by the announcement made by the government of Manitoba today. I want to say this to the federal government: under our legislation, when a dangerous disease is found anywhere in Canada and animals must be slaughtered and farmers compensated, it is the federal authority which has to assume responsibility and provide compensation for any losses that ensue. Consequently it seems to me that the action by certain provinces is a matter which should be carefully looked into by the government and the Department of Justice, so that the constitutional position of the dominion and the provinces may be reviewed carefully. Because I can foresee that if this is allowed to continue, and if cattle and other products from Alberta and Saskatchewan are stopped from moving across the country under conditions which are considered by the federal authority to remove any possibility of the spreading of the disease, two things will happen: first of all, the producers in the two western provinces will be cut off from any market. The result will be disastrous not only to those producers but to the whole of Canada.
The second point is this, that supplies of food for British Columbia as well as for the central and eastern provinces are to some


extent-and quite largely now, in some respects-dependent upon the movement of supplies from the two prairie provinces. I do not think the government can allow the stoppages to go unchallenged. I think the government has to take its responsibility. It must go into this matter very carefully indeed and see to it that the basis of confederation is maintained. And, as I understand it, that basis was that there would be a free flow of commodities without let or hindrance among all the provinces of Canada.
Since, as I say, the federal parliament- and I use the word "parliament" instead of "government"-assumes the responsibility in cases of this kind for the compensation of the owners of diseased animals, and for taking the necessary steps to deal generally with such situations, it seems to me that the provinces recognize that, at least financially, all matters affecting the disease of animals are a federal responsibility. And if that is so, then it seems that since the federal authority quarantines, and takes all the responsibility for assistance under such circumstances, the provinces are usurping the rights of this parliament and of the federal authority in preventing the flow of supplies, under proper conditions of inspection, and guarantee of good health, among the provinces. They are usurping the rights of this parliament in preventing the flow across this country of commodities that should have the right to move from one end of the country to the other.
I am hesitant to say that, but I think someone has to say it. Perhaps it will be said immediately that my views are those of one who believes in the centralization of authority in the federal parliament. I do not believe in that. As a matter of fact, I believe that the basis of democracy lies in a maximum of local self-government as it exists in the municipality, the province and so on. But I do believe this, that under the federal system agreed upon in 1867 we must beware lest people in one part of Canada-in this instance in two of the prairie provinces-be penalized because of actions that are beyond the constitutional right of the provinces as set forth in the British North America Act.
I am not a constitutional lawyer, but I believe the views I have expressed as a layman are sound views. They are in the interests of all Canada. And I believe further that in the interests of all Canada the federal government must take notice of the situation and take such action as may be appropriate at this time.

Some twenty farmers have had their livestock afflicted with this disease, but any farmer who has any livestock at all stands to lose because of the quarantine.
Everything said by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) about the action taken by the provinces is absolutely correct. If this government has certain powers under the constitution, as I believe it has, it should not stand idly by and let one province after another encroach on the powers of the federal government to the detriment of the citizens of other provinces. The whole surplus beef area of western Canada is being blocked off from the markets in the rest of Canada. Quite apart from the results of foot-and-mouth disease, there has been a drop of $10 per hundredweight in the price of beef during the last few months. I noticed from the Winnipeg Free Press of a few days ago that cattle were being quoted on that market at $24.50 per hundredweight for choice steers, down $10 during the last few months. If the government does not take action to provide a floor under the price of

beef, livestock prices will continue to go down and particularly in Saskatchewan, when the packing plants are reopened.
I submit that the government should consider appointing a controller to administer proper floor prices and to see that the packers pay proper floor prices. The farmer who produces beef should be maintained in production. As has been suggested by the hon. member for Battle River, the floor price should be to the producer and not to the packer, as has always been the case in the past with government floor prices.
This is a national emergency but this bill does not prove to me that the government believes it to be a national emergency. Nothing is being done to stabilize livestock prices throughout Canada. Nothing is being done by the government to stop the balkanization of Canada, as the action taken by different provinces has been called. It is time the government appointed a controller and fixed a decent and adequate floor under beef prices.
I hope the government will keep in mind that the income of farmers other than those who are directly affected by the disease is being curtailed. What about the farmer with perhaps fifty head of beef cattle who lives in the quarantine area? He is not able to market those cattle although some of them may be of market weight. There is no guarantee as to how long he will have to maintain those cattle on his farm before being able to realize any income from them. These farmers will not be able to move catle from one quarter-section of land to another. Mr. Speaker, I do not propose to take very much time to discuss this matter, because I believe the discussion should be confined within a very small compass. Times like these impress upon the people of this country the fact that when an emergency develops in any part of Canada, this parliament representing the whole of this country is always ready, willing and anxious to give assistance.
This bill does not deal with the right of the provinces to interfere with the transportation of livestock from one province to another. That is a constitutional matter. If those who have beef cattle, swine or anything else to export to other provinces are in any way hindered by the authorities of those provinces, it is up to them to get out and ascertain whether or not the provinces have the right to do that. I am not entering into a discussion of that question. Neither does this bill propose to stabilize any industry in this country. It only proposes to render compensation to those unfortunate people in the west who must have their herds slaughtered or their buildings destroyed because of this awful disease.
This method of rendering assistance in an emergency of this kind, by way of legislation, is something new in this country. When we had the tremendous tragedies of the Red river, the Fraser river and Rimouski, those matters were brought before the house under special circumstances, and parliament dealt with them and provided assistance. The farmers of this country are in a somewhat different category, and I think properly so. Many years ago the Animal Contagious Diseases Act provided compensation to farmers whose livestock had to be destroyed because of disease. I am presuming that before introducing the resolution on which this bill is founded the minister came to the conclusion that the remuneration provided under that legislation was not sufficient to cover the loss being suffered in the west today; and I think perhaps that is fair.
Until a moment ago I thought my good friend from Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) was going to introduce an amendment to this bill. This legislation deals only with two principles, or as a matter of fact only one principle. It deals with the method by which these people in the west whose livestock must be slaughtered are to be compensated. In the second place it deals with those people whose grain or buildings may be destroyed, and how they are to be compensated. I have great admiration for the good old principles of the common law in the matter of damages, and in my opinion the minister is bringing this legislation squarely within those principles.
How is compensation given? Under the common law in our courts, or in some instances under statutes which amend the common law, the basis is fair and reasonable compensation for the loss sustained by those bringing the action. That is what I mean by saying the minister has brought this legislation squarely within the principles of
