It has all the earmarks of being very hastily drawn. I am not going to be unduly critical of the government simply because the bill has been hastily drawn. It seems as though the subject has seized the government's attention in the serious way that it should for only a short time, and the bill seems to have been drafted with great haste.
It is regrettable in the first place, sir, that the terms of the bill are so nebulous, and also that it has the vice which so much government legislation has, that it confers powers upon the government without at the same time defining the rights of those whom parliament is seriously trying to help. One great and patent shortcoming of this bill, it seems to me, is that it does not adequately define the rights of those whom we are trying to help, namely those farmers whose possessions, whether in the form of livestock, buildings or other forms, are going to be affected, and others as well as the farmers who happen to be the owners of cattle or property affected.
It seems to me it is quite proper to give approval to the principle of this bill, as everyone who has spoken in this debate on second reading has done, and at the same time to be critical of the shortcomings of the bill in giving effect to a sound principle. The sound principle obviously is that in a national calamity of this kind, comparable with others that parliament has recognized, parliament should put the resources of the country into the breach. Let us look at this bill first of all in the terms of the scope of the principle, to ascertain the scope within which the sound principle is permitted to operate.
I point out in the first place that the bill gives recognition to claims only on the part of those who are owners of animals, fodder, grain or other things that are ordered to be destroyed. No one derives any compensation under the provisions of this bill unless either his animals, his buildings, his fodder or his grain or something, presumably some physical thing owned by him, is destroyed. It seems to me, on the face of it, that is a very inadequate scope to be given to the sound principle that all members have supported in the course of this debate.

Now, what about many others whose rights are going to be affected by the exercise of the rights conferred by this bill upon the minister or the rights conferred by the Animal Contagious Diseases Act upon the government, whose cattle are not going to be slaughtered, whose buildings, fodder or grain are not going to be destroyed. I venture to say that before this calamity has passed, important as will be the losses sustained by those whose cattle, buildings, fodder or grain will have been destroyed under the powers given by this bill, a greater aggregate loss is going to be sustained by those whose cattle and property will not have been destroyed. This bill makes no provision whatever for compensation for those persons. If we recognize, as I think all members do, that this is a national calamity and that parliament should act in the national interest, by what authority do we draw a line and say that compensation shall be given only to those whose cattle, buildings, fodder or grain are destroyed? What about those whose rights are very seriously curtailed, and whose property is seriously diminished in value by the exercise by the minister of the powers given to him under the Animal Contagious Diseases Act?
There are these sweeping quarantine orders, the effects of which are already being felt seriously and will continue to be felt by many farmers and many other persons in western Canada whose animals will not have been slaughtered or whose buildings, fodder or grain will not have been destroyed. It seems to me that, examined in the light of that principle, the scope of this bill is altogether inadequate. I urge upon the government, because it is only the government that can introduce a measure of this kind, to give the bill the scope it requires. I urge upon the government that it should extend the scope of the bill. It is not within the power of any private member in this house to introduce an amendment which will have the effect of increasing the expenditure through the avenue of compensation. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that in this situation it is the clear duty of the government to widen the scope of the bill so that those who are going to feel the effects of this bill, perhaps to the extent of serious losses by the exercise by the minister of his powers under this bill and the Animal Contagious Diseases Act, will also be entitled to compensation.
There is another aspect that does require serious attention on the part of the house, and it was stressed by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in what he had to say this evening as well as at earlier stages in the debate on this measure. I wish

I was addressing myself to the argument just advanced to the house by the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond (Mr. Carroll) who was at some pains to argue that the basis of compensation provided by this bill is adequate and in keeping with the principles of the common law. It was that argument in particular with which I was dealing, Mr. Speaker, without going into questions as to the specific details of compensation to be awarded.
I will not be long on the subject, but I was drawing to the attention of the minister the fact-which I do not think has been clearly recognized as yet in the discussion- that this bill makes provision, with regard to compensation for those whose animals are slaughtered, for slaughtering carried out under the provisions of this act. That provision will not bring any comfort at all to those who suffer losses as the result of acts performed under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. It seems to me, Mr. Speaker, that before we have left this subject we shall have to have a much clearer definition than is now provided for the determination of the relationship between those two measures.
As to the contention of the hon. member for Inverness-Richmond with regard to the recognition given by this act, in its essential principles, to the provisions of the common law, may I say this. With great respect for the hon. member-and I am sure everyone in this house has great respect for his legal learning-I argue that this bill does not justify that confidence. This bill does not give adequate effect to a proper principle. What adequacy can there be in compensation defined by this act with respect to individual animals, individual buildings or individual quantities of fodder or grain? That is what this bill deals with. This bill does not seek to deal with the situation where compensation can be awarded, in my submission, only on the basis of someone being in business as most of those whose property will be

destroyed under this act or the main act undoubtedly will be. It is one thing to take away an individual animal from a man and pay him adequate compensation for it; but, sir, it is an entirely different thing to destroy his whole herd, his whole physical capital. Compensation to be awarded on the basis of individual animals destroyed cannot possibly compensate a man whose whole herd is destroyed under conditions like that.
There is no provision here for principles such as those which are recognized under other federal legislation such as the Expropriation Act. There is no recognition here of the right of any person affected by this act to some specific compensation for forcible taking. This is not the case at all of the farmer marketing his own animals in his own way. This is the case of the government intervening, in the exercise of special powers conferred by extraordinary measures of this kind, and simply at one swoop taking his herd or his properties away from him. That is an entirely different situation from the one that is contemplated in the compensation sections of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act; and, with respect, I submit it is a different one from that provided for under the compensation provisions in this bill.
Only the government can introduce in this house amendments which will give to the principle of this measure the broadening effects which are necessary to provide for the persons in the categories recognized here an adequate measure or basis of compensation. "Fair and reasonable compensation" does not adequately define the type of compensation which should be recognized in this measure. The hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) has pointed out that it should not be left to rest within the judgment or discretion of a minister of the crown, even with the assistance of a board of valuators. What is required here is a much broader definition of, first of all, the categories of persons who are to receive a right to compensation under this act and, in the second place, a much wider definition of what it is for which compensation is to be provided.
This bill needs something in the way of a definite provision for rights of compensation on the part of those who may suffer loss or damage for, or by reason of, or in consequence of any act done or performed under the provisions of this legislation, or under the provisions of the Animal Contagious Diseases Act.
I say again that no private member of this house is permitted under the rules of the house, or under the provisions of the British

North America Act, to introduce the type of amendment that is required to give adequate effect to the principle of this legislation which we are now discussing. That burden and that responsibility rest on the government, and I urge upon the government to give adequate recognition to a principle which I think has been supported by all members of this house.

speakeroldname: Mr. George A. Drew (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, already you have indicated that there may be some difficulty in defining the exact points within which discussion should take place under the measure now bef ore us, and perhaps that difficulty in itself is emphasized by the wording which describes the legislation itself. It is described as:
An act for the control and extirpation of foot-and-mouth disease.
That is not what the legislation really is. That starts us off on a very difficult beginning. The control of foot-and-mouth disease is something that could have been carried out by the department if it had been doing its duty under existing laws. This is really legislation to give authority to the government to slaughter such animals as it believes should be slaughtered under these circumstances, and to provide a measure of recompense for the slaughtered animals. I am mentioning this at the outset because some of the remarks I propose to make are directed to the suggestion that this bill should be much wider than it now Is, and I would hope that consideration would still be given at this time to the widening of this bill to recognize that this problem is not simply one of paying adequate money to those whose animals are of necessity slaughtered; but that there are many other things that must be done if those who may suspect that there is foot-and-mouth disease on their farms are to be encouraged to report at the earliest possible moment.
That is what should be encouraged in every way within the power of the government and of parliament. As has been well pointed out already by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) in the remarks which he has made on this bill, the real purpose which should be in mind is to encourage in every way possible the closest and most effective co-operation between the farmers themselves and the various representatives of the government in whose hands this responsibility rests.
I do want to speak just for a moment about something that was mentioned by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) when he spoke a short time ago with regard to this bill. He spoke of the concern that
Foot-and-mouth disease he felt about the fact that here within this country provincial governments are setting up barriers which in effect may prevent that free movement between provinces which has been regarded as one of the essential requirements of a single and united nation. I suggest that the only reason that the provinces have found it desirable and necessary to place embargoes on the movement of cattle is that they are so convinced that this government has fallen down on its job that they are not going to take chances on continuing carelessness in this government in dealing with this serious matter. I suggest that if the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) had told hon. members what he could have told the house he would have been able to tell them why it was that the province of Quebec had acted so quickly. The information I have is that there were very definite reasons why the province of Quebec acted as quickly as they did. And in relation to that I would point out that no satisfactory answer has yet been given to the questions which have been asked about the reasons for the embargo placed on importation of cattle from the United States. In reporting the statements made by the Minister of Agriculture yesterday the Canadian Press indicated that the consensus was that this was not intended really as a barrier on the movement of cattle from the United States so much as it was intended as a device to force the provinces into submission to the wish of the Minister of Agriculture that they should abandon their embargoes. Not by one word, not by one suggestion, has the Minister of Agriculture attempted to remove the impression conveyed in the report carried yesterday in the Canadian Press dispatch. On the contrary there is very much to support that statement in what has been said here.
When he was challenged in regard to the danger that might be inherent in placing an embargo on the importation of cattle from the United States at a time when we were seeking their co-operation to be permitted to export cattle there as soon as possible, the Minister of Agriculture said last night in this house that really this did not mean a thing; that after all the United States was not going to be exporting cattle into Canada. He said in as clear words as he could possibly have used that, so far as the United States was concerned, it was not intended as an embargo. He knew perfectly well that, with the loss in value of animals in this country, there is going to be no substantial importation in any event of cattle from the United States at the prices that still obtain in that country. He recognizes, however, that the provinces of British Columbia and Quebec particularly, which do not produce the number of animals required for

Foot-and-mouth disease their needs, would be looking to the United States and to those boundary states from which they have been in the habit of drawing animals in times past, and that this embargo on the exportation from these states would be a very serious matter for the provinces in this country that found it necessary to import.
Unless there is some explanation given before we pass from second reading of this bill, no matter what the principle of it is, we pass it with the knowledge that in the various explanations which have been given we have really been told that this embargo is nothing but a club to force the provinces into submission. That suggestion carried by the Canadian Press is supported by the words used this afternoon by the Minister of Agriculture. He said, "Unfortunately some of the provinces have placed embargoes on the movement of cattle." "Unfortunately" is the word he used. He makes it clear that he does not want those embargoes, and I am sure most members of the house do not want to see embargoes. But we must remember that agriculture is one of the two things in the British North America Act made the subject of equal and co-ordinate jurisdiction. Agriculture is just as much within the hands of the provinces as it is within the hands of the dominion government.
Where the dominion government has failed to do its duty, as it has in this case, and where the dominion government has been guilty of the grossest negligence, as it has in this case, and where it has failed to do the things that should have been done to protect agricultural production in this country from this dreadful disease, and the spreading of it, then I submit the provinces of Canada, the provincial governments of this country, would be negligent in their duty if they failed to take whatever steps they regarded as proper to prevent the spread of the disease at a time when the dominion government was failing to carry out its duties in any very noticeable way.
May I qualify that statement only to this extent, that not one of us in the house wants barriers of this kind erected between provinces. Not one of us in the house wants to see established as a precedent the placing of any sort of impediment in the way of the free movement of agricultural or any other products within the boundaries of Canada as a nation. Nevertheless we must recognize the very natural concern in the minds of those who comprise the governments of the various provinces, and in the minds of the


officials of the provincial departments of agriculture, when they see that it takes the dominion government three months to diagnose a disease which every qualified veterinarian knows to be one of the dangerous diseases, and against which we should be on guard at all times.
I am not suggesting that this is not a difficult disease to diagnose. It is. That is taught in the veterinary colleges in this country. And in passing may I say there are no better veterinary colleges in the world than those in Canada. That is amply demonstrated by the fact that if anyone goes to a veterinary college in this country he will find in it young men from the United States, from South America, from Europe and other countries, who have come here because of the high standing of our colleges. The graduates of those colleges could diagnose this and other diseases. They are capable of doing it.
This disease is not something that creeps up on us in the night without warning as to its possibilities. On this continent it is a disease which has been guarded against with the utmost care. This disease has been endemic in Europe for many years. It is a disease that is rarely completely eradicated in many of the nations of Europe. That is particularly true after a great disturbance of population and of animals such as takes place in any major war of the kind that took place only a few years ago. But it has not been endemic either in the United States or in Canada. There was an outbreak in the United States some years ago, and in Canada we took great care to prevent its coming into this country.
But can we imagine any Canadian having much confidence if he were taught to believe that there is nothing surprising about taking three months to diagnose the disease? There would be little chance of protecting the borders of this country if in fact that were the actual situation. But there is not one of us who does not know that that is not so. And this is particularly true of the Minister of Agriculture.
In the 1942 Year Book of Agriculture, a United States publication, we find, in an article entitled "Keep Livestock Healthy", the following observations:
Humanj beings are next in importance to infected animals and animal products as agents responsible for the spread of the disease. It is generally believed that human beings convey the virus mechanically on the clothing or person.
In other words, in 1942 and in years long before that, it was recognized that next to the carriage of the disease by animals themselves, the clothing and belongings of human

beings were the most likely mechanical means by which this disease could be transported.
What has happened here? The Minister of Agriculture on different occasions during this debate, with that skilful distracting of attention which is one of his most noticeable characteristics in debate, suggested that some of the things that were being said would be inclined to alarm the people of this country. I say nothing that has been said here could alarm the people of this country nearly as much as has the negligence of the government. What has been said here has been said in an attempt to get some real assurance that the government not only recognizes its failure in this instance, but will make sure that similar failures will not occur elsewhere. But we have had no assurance of that-none whatever, not the slightest. On the contrary, we have had expressions of satisfaction to the effect that everything had been done.
Every member in the house should be greatly alarmed by the fact that the government has given no indication that it is learning from this disastrous lesson, and that it is going to take better methods for detecting this disease in other areas, if such outbreaks should occur. The minister said some of the dramatic statements that were made might cause alarm. What could be more dramatic than the cloak-and-dagger stories that were appearing as to the mounted police following this blond German back and forth across the country? Why, you had all the atmosphere of a dime thriller in the stories that were appearing when, it was said, the mounted police had traced him to Port Arthur. Then they thought he was on the way to Montreal, that he was somewhere in eastern Canada- and he was taken in Vancouver!
One question was not answered today. The Minister of Agriculture said that he would not want to use the Royal Canadian Mounted Police, when the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. . Diefenbaker) was pointing out that steps should have been taken much more quickly and more vigorously to obtain the information that was so greatly needed. No, they did not want to use the mounted police -but they had them chasing all over the country for one single German immigrant from Westphalia, who was welcomed by some inspector. He was brought over here, apparently, without much examination of his clothing, his intentions or anything else. And I say "his intentions" designedly.
Is it possible that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were brought into this for some reason other than the fear of disease? There were others who could have examined his clothing. The immigration branch has
Foot-and-mouth disease authority to do that. The Department of Citizenship and Immigration could have done a number of things to check this man. Is it possible that the Royal Canadian Mounted Police were interested in more than his clothing? If so, we should know it; because part of the trouble we have here if, in fact, this man was a carrier, is the careless manner in which so much of the immigration into this country has been handled within these last few months. Since this bill was introduced yesterday by consent we have been seeking to obtain some assurance from the government that it recognized the failure of its system and would give us assurances, which we as members have a right and, what is more, a solemn duty to demand in the face of a disaster of this kind.
This is something that we can find covered in authoritative books. May I quote again from the same textbook to which I have already referred, the 1942 Year Book of Agriculture, as follows:
Failure to recognize the disease when it exists might permit the extensive spread of the malady, perhaps to such a point that even radical methods would not eliminate it or would do so only at very great cost. On the other hand, to make an incorrect diagnosis of foot-and-mouth disease would mean unnecessarily imposing severe and costly quarantines and restrictions, locally, nationally, and internationally, in addition to needless slaughter of animals. In the United States, therefore, extreme caution is used in making a diagnosis.
That statement may be taken as indicating why the government should act with the utmost care before declaring that this is foot-and-mouth disease. Most certainly they should. And because they should is all the more reason why in no single case where one of the diseases so similar in symptoms is found should there be any doubt of any kind that it is not foot-and-mouth disease. They did not take steps in this case to remove that doubt. Let me quote further from this same textbook, as follows:
Only two other diseases cause inflammatory changes in the mucous membranes of the mouth or the skin of the feet or both in cattle, swine, sheep, goats, and other cloven-hoofed animals sufficiently similar to those of foot-and-mouth disease to give the experienced observer difficulty in establishing a diagnosis. These are the virus diseases, vesicular stomatitis and vesicular exanthema of swine.
That textbook states simply that there are only three diseases which are similar and which cause inflammatory changes in the mucous membranes of the mouth or the skin of the feet or both in cattle, swine, sheep, goats and other cloven-footed animals. The very fact that such care is taken to guard against this disease indicates the reason why every possible precaution should be taken

Foot-and-mouth disease where symptoms of this kind, that is, inflammatory changes in the mucous membranes of the mouth or skin of the feet of these animals, appear and not one chance taken that it may be foot-and-mouth disease.
As has been pointed out, and very obviously, what has happened has happened. Nothing we say here is going to change the fact that there is foot-and-mouth disease. What we are concerned about now is to be sure that those who discover the possibility of this disease are encouraged to disclose it and that every possible step is taken to prevent its spread elsewhere and in that way to assure the earliest possible detection.
When we realize that the elimination of this disease depends very largely on the prompt co-operation of the farmers themselves, we must admit that the bill should provide for whatever monetary loss is going to occur, in so far as is reasonably possible, to the farmers who may have this disease on their property. For that reason the bill should provide that payment should be made on the basis of the real economic value of the animal and that under no circumstances should it diminish the amount that would be paid under existing legislation. The value of dairy animals should toe based upon the record of production. Third, the bill should provide compensation for unborn calves and unborn pigs.
The bill should also provide for the payment of compensation in connection with feed, straw, buildings, land, et cetera, which may be destroyed as a preventive measure. This last point is important. If farmers are to be encouraged to act promptly then surely it is wise, when considering a disaster that may cost us hundreds of millions of dollars, to pay adequate sums by way of compensation so that these farmers will willingly come forward and disclose a disease which will result in the destruction not only of their animals but possibly of other valuable property which they own. Unless this disease reaches proportions which would be disastrous beyond anything we now imagine, the money involved in dealing adequately with a situation of this kind would be quite small compared with the extent of the disaster with which the farmers and people generally of this country are confronted.
I would point out that while this bill is designed particularly to provide for the slaughter of animals in the areas of infection and to recompense farmers whose animals are slaughtered, this disaster is by no means to be measured by the number of animals slaughtered. This disaster affects farmers right across the country. It is only natural that I should have a personal interest in this matter as the constituency of Carleton,


which I represent, and which is the rural area west of Ottawa, is one of the great cattle producing areas in this part of the country. Sums have been lost by owners of cattle in that constituency simply by virtue of the decrease in value of the animals.
This disaster affects every province where cattle breeding is a major industry. The extent of the disaster can be understood only when we realize the scale on which losses have already occurred. There are herds in Ontario which have decreased in value as much as $150,000 as a result of the outbreak of foot-and-mouth disease in western Canada. That indicates the scale on which this industry is carried on at this time in some parts of eastern Canada. It is no answer to say that this represents simply the present drop in value. We have nothing before us to suggest that we can expect at an early date that the situation will change in a manner that will restore the value of these great purebred herds.
This disaster-and it is a major disaster- calls for the utmost co-operation. May I point out that co-operation was extended in this house yesterday in the form of unanimous agreement to permit this legislation to be dealt with. There has been no delay in the discussion of this bill that has not been caused by the failure of the minister to give this house the information and the assurances we have been asking, which we are still asking and which* we have not yet received. No; this house is ready to co-operate. I am satisfied that every hon. member agrees with the principle that we should pass an act which will adequately compensate farmers whose animals and property-and I add "property"-are destroyed, so they may be encouraged to report any suspicious symptoms immediately without any attempt to dispose of their animals or property in the hope of avoiding financial loss. It is all very well to say, Oh well, no one should do that in any event, no matter what the law may be. Some of the farmers of this country are in a desperate situation, and it is our duty to see to it that they are encouraged to co-operate to the very limit in dealing with this matter.
I suggest also that it is far from satisfactory to be left with the simple statement by the minister that after he has gone to Regina and after he has done other things he may at some future time meet the provincial ministers of agriculture. Recognizing that these barriers now exist, which not one of us wants to see here in Canada, recognizing that provinces have felt impelled to impose embargoes because they believe the dominion government has failed in its responsibility and been grossly negligent, this is the time to overcome those difficulties by bringing together

the provincial ministers of agriculture, remembering that under our constitution they have equal jurisdiction with the federal minister in dealing with problems of this kind. Before another day passes the Minister of Agriculture should arrange for a meeting with all the provincial ministers, and agree upon a plan for fighting this dread disease in a way which will satisfy the provinces and at the same time encourage the movement at the earliest possible date of cattle which can be safely moved. As every hon. member knows, normally western Canada would soon be moving feeders to the east. It will be a very serious thing if they are not permitted to do so. That is one reason this conference should take place right away, so that these feeders can be moved to eastern Canada and that very important branch of the livestock industry maintained.
Then consideration should be given to an agreed plan for orderly marketing. When I say "agreed" I mean a plan agreed upon by the dominion and provincial ministers of agriculture under which orderly marketing can be carried on which will prevent a collapse in the price of these animals. I hope no Canadian will think any real advantage would be gained if he might for the moment get this meat at lower prices as the result of a disaster of this nature. In the end he would be paying very much higher prices, and for an obvious reason. If this market collapses and there is panic selling, the great breeding herds will be sacrificed; and as every hon. member knows it will take years to restore those breeding herds across this country which have built up this tremendous cattle industry. Therefore orderly marketing agreed upon by the dominion and provincial departments of agriculture is one of the essential requirements to maintain confidence in the minds of the farmers and to preserve those great breeding herds which are equal to any in the world in the quality of the animals they produce.
Now may I say a word about the board. Already much has been said about these loose and undefined powers. I agree with what has been said by the hon. member for Lake Centre and the other hon. members who have spoken of the very unsatisfactory provisions of this act, which simply tells the government to go ahead and do whatever it thinks wise. From what we have seen already we have no reason to believe that the government is too wise in its approach to this problem. We think this act should state some clear principle which will guide the board in making its decisions. Yesterday the minister said very correctly, and I hope he will remember it, that the government must accept responsibility. The government must
Foot-and-mouth disease accept the whole responsibility instead of trying to pass it off on departmental officials and private practitioners. It must remember that it was responsible for the breakdown of the system that had been set up to discover a disease of this kind. It is also the responsibility of the government to let the board and the farmers know on what principle the board will be acting. Otherwise they will have to make their rules from day to day. This is something like the vague international rules to which the minister referred today, which he did not even know about. I hope that statement in Hansard will be well quoted, because it is a gem. The minister said the rules were so secret that even he did not know about them; but under those rules we are sending our people to do these jobs.

The minister does not know the wording, yet under those rules, of which he does not know the wording, men are being given instructions. That indicates just why it is so necessary in this instance that the wording should be clear and the principle stated so the board may know what really are its duties and responsibilities.
May I make one suggestion in regard to that board, which may have been made already. I am sure the men whose names have been mentioned are of high standing and recognized ability; but I understand that not one is himself an expert in the breeding of purebred animals. Since the area directly affected, to which this measure will apply, has many purebred herds, it is essential that on that board there be a representative of the purebred livestock industry who can interpret the real economic value of animals of that kind when compensation is being fixed.
What I have said, Mr. Speaker, has been put forward in the hope that we might still obtain from the minister some assurance that steps are going to be taken which will give a feeling of confidence across this country. Instead of doing anything to reassure us he has given us greater reason than ever to be alarmed. The minister simply says the animals were examined and the disease was diagnosed as something else. They went back and again it was diagnosed as something else. But the fact remains that it was foot-and-mouth disease, and nothing can change that. It should be his job to make sure that the system that is now applied in the rest of the country to prevent the spread is one which will not give the same faulty answers already given, and is one which will immediately detect this disease and prevent its further

Foot-and-mouth disease spread. I have put forward suggestions which I hope are worthy of consideration, and I feel sure that even if it involves another day's delay, that delay would be better than passing an act which is not adequate in its provisions, and which will not provide that encouragement to the farmers to report the first suspicion of the disease which, in itself, is the key to early diagnosis.

I should like to say a few words, Mr. Speaker, perhaps not bearing directly on the principle of the bill, but since the debate has dealt with other matters 1 feel I should be allowed to say something on this subject. An extremely critical situation has developed in the northeast part of the province of Saskatchewan, which happens to take in part of my constituency. Manitoba has rendered a hard blow to the people in that region by imposing an embargo on livestock. This area ships anywhere from ten to one hundred cars per week over the line of railway into Dauphin, Manitoba. A lot of talking has been done here that was not necessary, and it has meant that the minister has not had a chance to try to remedy this situation which has developed.
The farmers in the area have hogs which will be overweight if they are kept another week or two. This will result in a loss for which there will be no recompense. I ask the minister to do something to relieve this situation which has developed within the last two or three days. The killing and marketing area for the northeast part of the province of Saskatchewan is Winnipeg. It is not Saskatoon, and it is not Regina. It is no place other than Winnipeg, and that has been so for the last fifty years. So fax as livestock are concerned this area is really a part of Manitoba. I would suggest that something be done as soon as possible, because next Saturday is the shipping day for the northeast part of the province of Saskatchewan.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE

I am sorry that I was not able to be in the house to listen to all the remarks of the leader of the opposition. I believe I have heard everything that has been said on the question by all the other speakers. The reason I was not here throughout the whole of the speech delivered by the leader of the opposition is that I was attempting to reach some decision, and to receive some advice from the other members of the government, as to how the suggestions made by the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. 

Diefenbaker), and agreed with by members of the other two groups, might be made effective. I believe I have reached agreement with the member for Lake Centre as to a wording which will carry out his intent and our intent in connection with his suggestion, namely the clarification of what we all agree is the meaning of the section.
I am sorry that 1 have to say, in reply to a question the hon. member asked me, that it will be impossible to accept the other suggestion. Probably the hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Fleming) was correct when he suggested that it would be out of order. Probably it would, but apart altogether from that, I do not think it would be wise to introduce that amendment.
Having said that, I should like to say a word or two concerning the final remarks of the leader of the opposition. We are naturally just as anxious as any member in the house to have arrangements made between ourselves and the provinces as soon as possible which will be satisfactory. I believe that any actions which have been taken by the provinces have been largely as a result of fear. I am not too sure that when people are afraid of something that may happen to them they, are going to pay too much attention to whether their actions are constitutional or otherwise. They are simply going to try to protect themselves in so far as they can. The thing of which these people are afraid is that there is a disease in a limited area among livestock that may spread into other parts of Canada. They want to make certain that the spreading of the disease is not going to be allowed; that is the first thing of which they want to be sure.
I believe that the setting up of the district and the setting up of methods under which animals that have been affected can be destroyed, and through which those that have come in contact with animals affected will also be destroyed, plus the fact that no attempt will be made to move those animals into other parts of Canada, should take care of any fears these people have that someone is going to do something which will permit the animals to move to other sections of Canada. We are intent upon getting that part of the arrangement carried out before we ask the people to co-operate with us to the fullest extent in the matter of moving livestock. We feel we have made a proper arrangement to have that carried out, and just as soon as we know we are in a position to prove that satisfactorily to the representatives of the different provinces we shall approach them. They have their own reasons for doing what they have done, and some of them may be very good reasons. Until we are in a position

to present our case in such a way that it will be satisfactory to them, I doubt very much if any good can come out of any meeting that might be arranged. I can assure the house that just as soon as that set-up is properly arranged, and all actions are being taken in order to assure that no livestock will get out of that area into other parts of Canada, such a gathering will be held. Any trip that I may make to the west at the moment is just for the purpose of making certain, as between ourselves and the province that is concerned with the area, that we are satisfied that what I have just suggested is being properly carried out within the area. As soon as possible after that, we shall have the other gathering.
With regard to the purpose of this particular measure which has to do with the payment of compensation within the area, may I say that it is not concerned with the payment of compensation anywhere else. It has to do with the payment of compensation in the area where the disease actually exists, the area which is under quarantine. This area is practically all within twenty-five miles of Regina in one direction or another.

As a matter of fact, that is aU it covers at the moment. If the disease were to break out fifty miles away or five hundred miles away from that area, I would only then be in a position to take in those areas action similar to the action provided for in this district. I do not think that I can do that under the act, and I certainly would not feel that I had the authority to do it under the act as it is drafted.
On the question as to whether the compensation will be sufficient to make people feel that they ought to report the disease, may I say that I would not have been surprised had all the members made the same criticism as was made by the hon. member from Nova Scotia. I have heard the criticism so often in the house that I rather expected that the criticism would run more in that direction than in any other, and I appreciate the fact that it has not. I refer to the criticism that the payment would probably be too great rather than otherwise. I appreciate the fact that the house has not taken that
Foot-and-mouth disease position on this occasion. They have done so on other occasions when I have had to do with payments in the western part of Canada. On this occasion, however, their suggestion is that I may not pay enough. I do not think there is much reason for the argument. I think an effort will be made to pay what is fair and reasonable, and nothing more. I think that is all that these farmers will expect; and I am quite sure that the greater part, if not all, of them will be satisfied with the treatment they receive under the provisions of this measure.
The only thing I think I should say in addition to that is that there is some concern expressed on the part of some members- I think it was particularly expressed by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue) and by the hon. member for Melfort (Mr. Wright); and their expressions of opinion were agreed with by some others-that there are others who are going to be suffering.
We have done a few things which have been commended by hon. members in various parts of the house. The hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Ferrie) just referred to the fact that there would be hogs which would have to remain on farms for the next two or three weeks, or might have to remain there because of what the Manitoba government has done. We anticipated that situation when we changed our whole regulations with regard to grading and the payment of premiums on hogs, and have already intimated to all persons who might be inconvenienced in that regard that the heavier hogs will be graded in such a manner as to make possible payment on heavier hogs. As I say, we have been commended for that action in various parts of the house, and it does partially take care of the problem in the northeast for a limited time but not for a very long time. We therefore feel that something has been done in that direction.
As to other economic difficulties of persons both inside and outside the area, we all realize that there is no way in which the coming of foot-and-mouth disease to this country can assist us. There may be a few who will get higher prices in some limited communities for a short time because of the fact that the disease has come among us; but in the long run we are all going to lose by the fact that it has come. There is not anybody who is going to make anything by it. We shall all be in the same boat. Business is going to lose by it. Our transportation companies are going to lose by it. The farmers are going to lose by it. Everyone is going to lose by it. When we are all losing by any particular calamity that may come upon us, it is difficult to work out a plan under

Foot-and-mouth disease which we can all try to help one another in the sense that we are going to bring more financial remuneration to one another by what we do. In other words, what we are called upon to do is to try to see to it that one group of people in Canada are not injured to the benefit of others, and that those who are going to suffer some economic disadvantages are helped as far as possible.
In spite of what was said a few moments ago by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Drew), in closing the boundary line of Canada to the importation of meat and livestock the government have no other objective than to make it possible for the producers in Canada to have access to the only market there is for them for the time being. If in the long run it becomes possible to find a market somewhere else, that restriction can be removed from people outside Canada. It is not a restriction on people inside Canada. If we all co-operate in having the food that we have properly distributed to one another, there is no hardship in it for anybody in Canada. But if it becomes a hardship for people, say, in Australia, in that they cannot for the time being sell mutton and lamb in Canada, then in due course we would see to it at the earliest possible date that it is not a hardship even upon those people. But for the time being I am sure that people in Australia, in New Zealand, in the United States and elsewhere will realize that this is a problem with which we must deal in Canada, and that for the time being they may have to put up with any little hardships that they are required to put up with in order that we may deal with this particular problem. There is not any other objective whatsoever in the mind of the government in connection with the matter than to retain for the producers in Canada the one market which is available.
It is obvious to everyone that at the present time there is not sufficient demand in that market to take care of all of our cattle and of all of our hogs. That is obvious to everyone who looks at the facts. For the time being we are therefore not asking the consumers to undergo any hardship because they are not going to be able to get food. The food is here and available. The only way in which they can suffer any hardship is by people putting obstructions in the way of the distribution of food that is properly protected against any disease that there may be in the country.

The amendment provides for spending more money than is already provided for in the bill, and I think it is obvious to everyone that there is a definite ruling on that point in connection with amendments.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: The question of whether this is in order has been raised, and even that may involve some discussion. I am not going to discuss it now-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: The point the minister has made is quite obvious.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: -but it is eight minutes after eleven now, and I do not think we can finish the bill tonight, though I would like to do it. There may even be some discussion on third reading.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: In spite of what has been said in the house and particularly from the opposition side, to the effect that we have not been handling this thing as it might have been handled, for the last four nights I have had to work long after midnight and be back here for work again the next day. If the committee does not want to clean it up and get it into operation, all right; but I think we ought to go ahead and clean it up.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
Perhaps I should give my ruling now. Either this amendment
Foot-and-mouth disease involves increased expenditure or in my opinion it is absolutely valueless. There is a well known rule in that connection cited in paragraph 437 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition:
No principle is better understood than the constitutional obligation that rests upon the executive government, of alone initiating measures imposing charges upon the public exchequer.
Then in paragraph 453 at page 171 a well known rule is cited which appears in the Journals of 1949:
The tendency has been in the Canadian House of Commons for the past twenty-five years, to rule out all motions purporting to give the government a direct order to do a thing which cannot be done without the expenditure of money.
Regretfully I must rule this amendment out of order because, as I said, either it means an increase in expenditure or it is absolutely valueless.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Eleven o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: Shall section 2 as amended carry?

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman. Now that there is no question about the correctness of the objection raised, the minister having said that the result of the amendment would be that a larger amount of money would have to be paid out of the treasury than otherwise would be the case, it indicates that the farmers are not going to be properly compensated under this act and that the economic value of the animals is not going to be paid. That is one thing we intend to contend for, and the only way we can do so is by moving on third reading that the matter be referred back so that this house will have an opportunity of voting on whether or not the farmers are to be compensated for the economic value of their animals.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR CONTROL AND EXTIRPATION OF FOOT-AND-MOUTH DISEASE
speechtext:
I have a further amendment to move. The hon. member for Lake Centre has indicated that he intends to call a division on third reading. Therefore I would ask you to call it eleven o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I do not think it is reasonable to expect us to sit until twelve o'clock, which would be the earliest a vote could be taken. As a matter of fact unless the minister accepts the amendment I am going to move I expect I will find it necessary also to call for a vote on third reading, on the amendment I intend to suggest.
Section stands.
Progress reported.
It being ten minutes after eleven o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
